The function compares two NUL-terminated byte strings and reports their ordering, with an optional case-insensitive mode. The first and second arguments are pointers to the strings to compare. The third argument is a boolean flag: when true, comparison is case-sensitive; when false, ASCII letters are compared case-insensitively.

If either pointer is NULL, the function returns 1 immediately, without comparing any characters. If both pointers refer to the same address, it returns 0.

For case-sensitive comparison, the result is the standard lexicographic ordering of the two strings: a negative value if the first string sorts before the second, zero if they are equal, and a positive value if the first sorts after the second.

For case-insensitive comparison, corresponding characters are converted to lowercase before comparison. The function returns zero when the strings are equal ignoring case, including when both are empty. Otherwise it returns the numeric difference between the lowercase value of the first differing character in the first string and the corresponding character in the second string. This value is negative if the first string sorts before the second, positive if it sorts after.

The function does not modify either string, allocate memory, or alter any global state.

description:
The function compares one path element from each of two JSON pointer strings, returning a boolean result. The first argument is a string containing a path element to compare. The second argument is a string containing a path element that may use JSON pointer escape sequences. The third argument is a flag selecting whether letter case is significant.

Both arguments must be non-NULL; if either is NULL, the function returns false immediately.

The comparison proceeds character by character until a NUL terminator is reached in either string, or until a slash is encountered in the second argument. A slash in the second argument marks the end of that path element and is not compared. Within the second argument, a tilde introduces an escape sequence: a tilde followed by the digit zero represents a literal tilde, and a tilde followed by the digit one represents a literal slash. Any other character after a tilde is invalid and causes the function to return false. When an escape sequence is present, the corresponding character in the first argument must match the unescaped character.

For ordinary characters, the function compares them directly when the third argument indicates that letter case is significant; otherwise it compares them without regard to case. A mismatch at any point returns false.

After the loop, the function checks whether both strings ended at the same logical position. If one string has ended while the other still has a non-slash character remaining, the function returns false. Otherwise it returns true. The function has no side effects.

The function copies a NUL-terminated byte string from the second argument into the buffer pointed to by the first argument, applying JSON pointer escape encoding to two characters. The first argument must point to writable memory large enough to hold the encoded result, including its terminating NUL. The second argument must point to a valid NUL-terminated string.

Each byte is copied unchanged except for the two special cases. A forward slash is replaced by a tilde followed by the digit one. A tilde is replaced by a tilde followed by the digit zero. All other bytes, including any other non-printable or high-bit bytes, are copied as-is. The encoding is applied in a single left-to-right pass, so a tilde that is produced as part of an escape sequence is not itself re-escaped.

After the entire source string has been processed, a NUL byte is written immediately after the last encoded byte. The source string is not modified, and no memory is allocated or released. The destination buffer is not checked for sufficient size; if it is too small, memory beyond it is overwritten. The function returns nothing.

The function locates a JSON node within a tree and returns a JSON Pointer string describing the path from a starting node to that target node.

The first argument is the node from which the search begins; it may be an object, an array, or a leaf. The second argument is the node being searched for. Both must be non-NULL; if either is NULL, the function returns NULL.

If the two arguments refer to the same node, the function returns a newly allocated empty string.

Otherwise, the function recursively examines the children of the starting node. For arrays, each child is identified by its zero-based index. For objects, each child is identified by the string stored in its name member, with certain characters escaped according to JSON Pointer rules. The returned path begins with a slash, followed by the index or encoded name, followed by the remainder of the path found in the child.

The returned string is always newly allocated and must be released by the caller. If the target is not found anywhere in the subtree, the function returns NULL. If memory allocation fails at any point, the function returns NULL and releases any intermediate path strings it had allocated. If the starting node is neither an array nor an object but has children, the search still descends into them; however, if a matching child is found under such a non-container node, the function returns NULL after freeing the intermediate result.

The function retrieves an element from a linked list of children stored inside a container structure. The first argument points to the container; if it is null, the function returns null. The second argument is a zero-based index indicating which child to return.

The function walks the list starting at the first child. For an index of zero, it returns the first child. For larger indices, it advances through the list that many times and returns the node reached. If the index is greater than or equal to the number of children, the walk reaches the end of the list and the function returns null.

The function does not modify the container, the list, or any child. It does not allocate or free memory. It performs no error reporting and has no side effects. The returned pointer, when non-null, points to an existing child node owned by the container; the caller must not free it. The function is safe to call with a null first argument, in which case it returns null regardless of the index. It also handles an empty list by returning null for any index.

The function parses a non-negative decimal integer from a string that represents part of a JSON pointer array index. The first argument points to a NUL-terminated string of unsigned characters. The second argument points to a size_t object that will receive the parsed value.

The function accepts only strings that consist entirely of decimal digits, or digits followed by a slash character or the NUL terminator. A slash or NUL terminator marks the end of the index and is not consumed. The string must contain at least one digit. Leading zeroes are rejected unless the entire index is exactly the single digit zero; thus a string beginning with zero and followed by another digit or a slash is invalid.

If the string is valid, the parsed numeric value is stored in the object pointed to by the second argument, and the function returns 1. If the string is invalid — because it is empty, contains a non-digit before a terminator or slash, or has a leading zero followed by another digit — the function returns 0 and does not modify the object pointed to by the second argument.

The function does not check for numeric overflow; values larger than the maximum representable size_t wrap according to unsigned arithmetic. It performs no memory allocation and has no other side effects.

The function removes one element from a doubly linked list of child nodes stored inside the structure pointed to by the first argument. The second argument is a zero-based index selecting which child to remove.

The first argument must point to a valid structure that owns a child list. The function assumes the list links are consistent. The second argument may be any non-negative value.

The function walks the child list from its first element until it reaches the requested index or the end of the list. If the index is out of range, the function returns NULL and leaves the list unchanged.

If the requested element exists, the function unlinks it from the list by updating the previous and next links of its neighbors. When the removed element is the first child, the owning structure’s child pointer is advanced to the following element. When the removed element is the last child, the previous link of the new first child is updated to point to the new last element. The removed element’s own previous and next links are then set to NULL so it no longer references the list.

The function returns a pointer to the removed element. The caller gains ownership of that element; it is no longer part of the list, and its previous and next links are NULL. No memory is freed, and no other fields of the removed element or the owning structure are modified.

The function inserts an item into a linked-list array at a specified zero-based position. The first argument points to the array structure, whose first member points to the first child item in a doubly linked list. The second argument is the target index. The third argument points to the item to insert.

The function walks the list from the first child until it reaches the requested position or the end of the list. If the requested index lies beyond the end of the array, the function returns the integer zero and does not modify the array or the item.

If the requested index equals the current number of items, the item is appended at the end using the helper that adds an item to an array, and the function returns the integer one.

Otherwise, the item is linked into the list immediately before the item currently at the target position. The new item’s forward link is set to that existing item, its backward link is set to the existing item’s previous neighbor, and the existing item’s backward link is updated to point to the new item. If the insertion occurs at the beginning of the list, the array’s first-child pointer is updated to the new item; otherwise, the previous neighbor’s forward link is updated to point to the new item. The function then returns the integer one.

The function assumes the first argument is not NULL and points to a valid array structure, and that the third argument is not NULL. It does not allocate or free memory, and it does not alter the contents of the inserted item beyond its two link members.

The function retrieves a member from a JSON object by name. The first argument is a pointer to the object to search; it is assumed to be non-NULL and to represent an object value. The second argument is a pointer to a NUL-terminated string giving the name of the member to find; it is assumed to be non-NULL. The third argument is a boolean flag controlling whether the name comparison distinguishes uppercase and lowercase letters.

If the third argument is true, the search compares member names exactly, honoring letter case. If it is false, the search ignores case differences when matching names.

The return value is a pointer to the matching member if one is found. If no member with the given name exists, or if the first argument is not an object, the function returns NULL. The returned pointer refers to memory owned by the object and remains valid until the object is modified or freed; the caller must not free it.

The function does not modify the object, does not allocate or release memory, and has no other side effects. If multiple members share the same name, the one returned is the first encountered in the object's internal order.

description:
The function replaces the contents of an existing JSON node with a copy of another node, releasing any resources held by the target before the copy occurs.

The first argument is a pointer to the node to be overwritten. If it is null, the function does nothing and returns immediately. Otherwise, the function assumes the pointer is valid.

The second argument is passed by value and represents the source node. Its fields are copied into the target node, so the target becomes an independent copy of the source’s scalar data and pointers. No deep copy is performed on the source’s pointer members; the target simply adopts the same pointer values.

Before copying, the function frees three resources owned by the target, if they are non-null: the node’s name string, its value string, and its child node. The child node is deleted recursively, meaning its entire subtree is released. The name and value strings are freed individually. The target’s other fields, including numeric values, type, and sibling links, are not freed or otherwise processed before being overwritten.

After these releases, the raw memory of the target node is overwritten with the raw bytes of the source. This includes all pointer fields, so the target now references the source’s strings and child, if any. The source itself is not modified or freed. The function returns no value.

The comparison is performed case-sensitively for string values. The exact format of each element is determined by the internal comparison routine, but the array is empty when the two structures are equivalent.

description:
The function scans a NUL-terminated string and returns a pointer to the first position that satisfies one of three stopping conditions: the end of the string, a character listed in the second argument, or, when inline comments are enabled, the start of an inline comment.

The first argument is the string to scan. It must be a valid pointer to a NUL-terminated character sequence. The second argument is a pointer to a NUL-terminated string of characters to search for; it may be NULL, in which case no character set is considered and only the end of the string or an inline comment can stop the scan.

The return value is a pointer into the first argument. If a character from the second argument is found, the returned pointer points to that character. If no such character is found and inline comments are enabled, the scan also stops at the first character of an inline comment prefix, provided that the immediately preceding character in the string is whitespace. The returned pointer then points to that prefix character. If neither condition is met before the end of the string, the returned pointer points to the terminating NUL character.

The function does not modify the input string, allocate memory, or alter any global state. It treats characters as unsigned when testing for whitespace. The scan proceeds from the beginning of the string and stops at the earliest position that satisfies any applicable condition.

The function copies a string into a caller-provided buffer, guaranteeing NUL-termination when the buffer size is at least one byte. The first argument points to the destination buffer, the second to the source string, and the third gives the total capacity of the destination buffer in bytes.

The source is copied byte by byte until either its terminating NUL is reached or the destination has no room for another character before the final terminator. At most one fewer than the buffer size characters are copied. A NUL terminator is always written at the next position. If the source is shorter than the buffer capacity minus one, copying stops at the source’s terminator and no padding bytes are written. If the source is at least as long as the buffer capacity minus one, the buffer is filled with that many characters and then terminated, producing a truncated but valid string.

The function assumes the destination buffer is valid for writing and has at least the given size in bytes, and that the source string is readable and NUL-terminated. Behavior is undefined if the size is zero. No memory is allocated or freed, and no global state is modified. The function returns the first argument, the pointer to the destination buffer, after the copy and termination are complete.

The function opens a file for reading and delegates parsing of its contents to another routine, then closes the file and returns the parsing outcome.

The first argument is a NUL-terminated string giving the path of the file to open. The second argument is a callback function that will be invoked by the parsing routine for each configuration entry encountered. The third argument is an opaque pointer passed through unchanged to that callback on every invocation.

If the file cannot be opened, the function returns -1 immediately and does not invoke the callback.

If the file opens successfully, the function calls the parsing routine with the open file stream, the callback, and the opaque pointer. The return value of that call is preserved. After the parsing routine returns, the file is closed. The function then returns the preserved value, whatever it is.

The function itself performs no parsing, allocates no memory, and does not modify the callback or the opaque pointer. It does not alter the contents of the file. The callback may be invoked zero or more times, depending on the file contents and the behavior of the parsing routine. The function does not define the meaning of the callback's return value; it simply propagates the parsing routine's result to its caller.

The function reads the next line from a string buffer, behaving like the standard line-input function but operating on an in-memory source rather than a file.

The first argument is a writable character buffer that receives the line. The second argument is the maximum number of characters to place into that buffer, including the terminating null character. The third argument points to a context structure that tracks the current position in the source string and the number of characters remaining to be read.

The function returns the first argument on success, or NULL if no characters are read. It fails when the context indicates that no input remains, or when the maximum length is less than two, since at least one character plus a terminator must fit.

On success, the function copies characters from the source into the destination buffer until one of three conditions occurs: the source is exhausted, a line-ending character is copied, or the buffer is filled to one less than the maximum length. The line-ending character, if encountered, is included in the output. The destination buffer is always null-terminated after copying.

The context structure is updated to reflect the new source position and the remaining character count, even when the function fails due to insufficient buffer size. No memory is allocated or freed, and no other side effects occur.

The function parses INI-format text supplied directly from memory. The first argument points to the beginning of the text buffer, and the second argument gives the number of bytes available. The buffer need not be NUL-terminated; parsing stops after the given byte count is consumed or when the logical end of the INI content is reached.

The third argument is a callback that receives each parsed logical item: a section header, a key–value pair, or a comment. The fourth argument is an opaque pointer passed through unchanged to every callback invocation. The callback’s return value controls parsing: a nonzero return stops parsing immediately and becomes this function’s return value.

The function returns zero when the entire input is processed successfully. If the callback returns nonzero, that value is returned and parsing stops at that point. If the input is malformed, the function returns a negative error code; the specific negative value distinguishes the first error encountered, such as an invalid section header, a missing equals sign in a key–value line, or an out-of-memory condition during internal allocation. When an error occurs, no further callbacks are invoked, and any partially constructed item is discarded.

The function performs no I/O and does not modify the input buffer. It may allocate temporary memory internally, which is released before returning. The callback receives pointers into the input buffer or into temporary storage valid only for the duration of that callback invocation.

The function reserves the next unused slot in a caller-provided array of token structures and returns a pointer to it, or reports exhaustion.

The first argument points to parser state that tracks how many slots have already been handed out. The second argument points to the start of the token array. The third argument gives the total number of elements in that array.

If the count of already-allocated tokens has reached or exceeded the array capacity, the function returns NULL and changes nothing except leaving the parser state as it was. Otherwise, it selects the element at the position indicated by the allocation counter, then increments that counter by one.

The selected token is initialized to a neutral state: its type is set to the undefined enumeration value, its start and end offsets are both set to -1, and its size is set to 0. If the build enables parent links, the parent index is also set to -1.

The function returns a pointer to the initialized token. It performs no memory allocation or deallocation, does not modify the array beyond the single selected element, and does not alter any other parser fields. The returned pointer remains valid as long as the caller keeps the array and does not reuse that slot.

The function initializes a token structure with the supplied type and boundary positions. The first argument points to the structure to be filled; it must not be NULL. The second argument is the token type value to store in the structure's type member. The third and fourth arguments are the start and end offsets, respectively, that define the token's span; they are stored as given, with no validation or adjustment.

The function sets the structure's type member to the second argument, its start member to the third argument, its end member to the fourth argument, and its size member to zero. If the structure has an optional parent member, that member is left unchanged.

The function returns nothing. It performs no allocation, no error checking, and no other side effects beyond modifying the structure pointed to by the first argument. All inputs are accepted as-is, including negative offsets or a zero or negative span; the caller is responsible for ensuring the values are meaningful. The size member is always reset to zero regardless of any previous value.

The function scans a JSON primitive value starting at the current position of the parser state passed as the first argument. The second argument is the input buffer, and the third argument is its length. The fourth argument is an array of token structures, and the fifth argument is the number of elements in that array.

The function assumes the parser position is within the buffer and that the input is NUL-terminated. It advances until it encounters a terminator: whitespace, a comma, a closing square bracket, or a closing curly brace. In non-strict mode, a colon also terminates a primitive. If it reaches the end of the buffer without finding a terminator, it resets the parser position and returns the error value for an incomplete token. If it encounters a control character below ASCII 32 or a byte at or above ASCII 127 before a terminator, it resets the parser position and returns the error value for invalid input.

If the token array pointer is NULL, the function backs up the parser position by one and returns zero without storing a token. Otherwise, it requests a new token from the token array. If no token is available, it resets the parser position and returns the out-of-memory error value. On success, it fills the new token with the primitive type, the starting position, and the position of the terminating character, records the current parent token index if parent links are enabled, backs up the parser position by one, and returns zero.

The first argument is the parser state; the second is the input buffer; the third is the buffer length; the fourth is an optional token array; the fifth is its capacity.

The function advances past the opening quote and scans until an unescaped closing double quote, a NUL byte, or the end of the buffer. Backslash escapes are validated: allowed single-character escapes are double quote, forward slash, backslash, b, f, r, n, and t. A backslash followed by u must be followed by exactly four hexadecimal digits. Any other escape is invalid.

If the fourth argument is NULL, the function still validates the string and returns zero on success without storing a token. Otherwise, on success it allocates one token from the supplied array, fills it with the string type, sets its start just after the opening quote and its end at the closing quote, and returns zero. If the token array is full, it restores the parser position to the opening quote and returns the out-of-memory error value.

On an invalid escape, it restores the parser position and returns the invalid-input error value. If the buffer ends or a NUL byte appears before a closing quote, it restores the parser position and returns the partial-input error value.

The function initializes a parser object so that it is ready to begin parsing a new JSON input. It takes one argument, a pointer to a parser structure, which must not be NULL. The function assumes the pointed-to structure is valid and writable.

It resets the parser’s internal state by setting three fields. The first field, which tracks the current byte offset within the input being parsed, is set to zero. The second field, which counts how many tokens have been produced so far, is also set to zero. The third field, which records the index of the parent token or container currently open, is set to negative one, indicating that no container is open and the parser is at the top level.

The function returns nothing. It performs no memory allocation or deallocation, does not modify any global state, and has no side effects other than writing to the structure pointed to by its argument. It does not validate the pointer beyond requiring it to be non-NULL, and it does not inspect or alter any input buffer. After the call, the parser is in a clean initial state, ready to accept a new buffer and token array for a fresh parsing session.

The function creates and returns a new input object representing an in-memory string source. The first argument is a file name or label associated with the input; it is assumed to be a valid NUL-terminated string and is copied into the new object. The second argument is the input text itself, also assumed to be a valid NUL-terminated string, and it is copied as well.

The returned object is dynamically allocated. Its type is set to the string-input kind. The stored file name and input text are independent copies, so later changes to the caller’s strings do not affect the object. The object’s initial parsing position is set to the start of the input, with row and column at their beginning values and no termination flag set.

The object is initialized for backtracking: backtracking is enabled, suppression is off, and the mark stack is empty but has an initial capacity of 32 entries. The last consumed character is recorded as the NUL character. The memory table used for memoization is marked as entirely unused, with its index set to zero.

No file or pipe handle is opened; the corresponding fields are set to null. The function does not validate the arguments beyond assuming they are non-null, and it does not report errors. If any allocation fails, the behavior is undefined. The caller owns the returned object and is responsible for eventually freeing it and its internal copies.

Otherwise, the function tries to satisfy the request from the context’s pool.
