The object’s initial parsing position is set to the start of the input, with row and column at their beginning values and no termination flag set.

The object is initialized for backtracking: backtracking is enabled, suppression is off, and the mark stack is empty but has an initial capacity of 32 entries. The last consumed character is recorded as the NUL character. The memory table used for memoization is marked as entirely unused, with its index set to zero.

No file or pipe handle is opened; the corresponding fields are set to null. The function does not validate the arguments beyond assuming they are non-null, and it does not report errors. If any allocation fails, the behavior is undefined. The caller owns the returned object and is responsible for eventually freeing it and its internal copies.

rejected_text:
The function allocates a block of memory of the requested size. The first argument points to an input context that maintains a pool of small fixed-size memory slots; the second argument is the number of bytes to allocate.

If the requested size exceeds the size of one pooled slot, the function returns a pointer from the standard allocator, with no other effect on the context.

Otherwise, the function tries to satisfy the request from the context’s pool. It examines slots starting at the current pool index, wrapping around the pool as needed, and selects the first slot that is marked free. That slot is then marked as occupied, the current pool index is advanced to the slot after the selected one, and a pointer to the slot’s storage is returned. The contents of the returned storage are not initialized.

If every slot in the pool is already occupied, the function falls back to the standard allocator and returns a pointer from it. In that case the pool state is unchanged except that the current pool index may have wrapped during the search.

The function never returns NULL on its own; if the standard allocator fails, its NULL result is passed through. It does not release memory, modify the input string or file state, or alter any other part of the context. The returned pointer remains valid until the corresponding deallocation function is called or, for pooled slots, until the slot is reused.

description:
The function moves a memory allocation out of the input object’s internal memory pool so that it survives independently of that input object.

The first argument points to the input object whose memory pool is consulted. The second argument is a pointer to a block of memory that may or may not be managed by that pool.

The function first checks whether the second argument is currently tracked as a pool allocation. If it is not, the pointer is returned unchanged and no other action is taken.

If the pointer is tracked, the function allocates a new block of the same fixed size used for pool entries, copies the contents of the original block into the new block, and then releases the original pool allocation. The newly allocated block is returned.

The returned pointer therefore always points to memory with the same contents as the second argument. The only observable difference is whether that memory remains managed by the input object’s pool or becomes an independent allocation. If the second argument was not pool-managed, the returned pointer equals the second argument. If it was pool-managed, the returned pointer is a distinct allocation that the caller becomes responsible for releasing.

The function does not modify the contents of the pointed-to memory. It may free the original pool allocation in the managed case. No other side effects occur.

The function records a backtracking checkpoint for an input object passed as its first argument. If the object’s backtracking capability is disabled, the function returns immediately without any effect.

When backtracking is enabled, the function increments the count of stored checkpoints. If the current storage capacity is insufficient, it expands two internal arrays: one holding parser state snapshots and one holding the most recent character values. The new capacity is the new checkpoint count plus half of that count, rounded down. Both arrays are resized to that capacity.

The function then stores the current parser state, consisting of position, row, column, and termination flag, into the state array at the slot corresponding to the new checkpoint count. It also stores the most recently consumed character into the parallel character array at the same slot.

If the input source is a pipe and this is the first checkpoint recorded, the function allocates a one-byte buffer initialized to zero and assigns it to the input object’s buffer. This allocation occurs only under those combined conditions.

The function returns no value. It may allocate memory, and if allocation fails, the standard allocator’s failure behavior applies. Existing checkpoints and the input object’s other fields are otherwise left unchanged.

The function removes the most recently recorded backtracking mark from the input object passed as its only argument. If fewer than one mark is currently recorded, it returns immediately without changing anything.

Otherwise, it decrements the count of active marks by one. It then checks whether the allocated capacity for marks is more than one and a half times the new count, and also above a fixed minimum capacity. If both conditions hold, it shrinks the capacity to the larger of the new count and that minimum, reallocating the two parallel arrays that store mark states and associated character data. The contents of the retained entries are preserved.

If the input source is a pipe and the new mark count is zero, the function pushes back all characters currently held in the internal buffer onto the underlying stream, in reverse order so the original sequence is restored. It then frees the buffer and sets the pointer to it to NULL.

The function returns no value. It may allocate or free memory as part of resizing the mark storage or clearing the pipe buffer. No other externally visible state is modified.

The function records that one input character has been successfully consumed and advances the parse position accordingly. The first argument points to the input state, which must be valid. The second argument is the character being consumed. The third argument is an optional pointer to a location where a newly allocated string containing that character should be stored.

If the input source is a pipe, the internal buffer exists, and the buffer is not currently in range, the function enlarges the buffer by two bytes, appends the consumed character, and terminates the buffer with a null character. The exact ordering of these buffer modifications is not observable except through the final contents.

The function then updates the stored last character to the consumed character, increments the absolute position and the column position, and, if the consumed character is a newline, resets the column to zero and increments the row.

If the third argument is not null, the function allocates a two-byte block, places the consumed character in the first byte and a null terminator in the second, and stores the address of that block in the location pointed to by the third argument. The caller owns this allocation.

The function always returns the integer value 1. It does not reject any input character and does not report errors.

The function attempts to match a literal sequence of characters against the current input stream. The first argument is the input context. The second argument is a NUL-terminated string containing the characters to match. The third argument points to a location where a newly allocated copy of that string will be stored on success.

The function first records the current input position. It then examines each character of the second argument in order. For each character, it tries to consume the same character from the input. If any character cannot be consumed, the input position is restored to the recorded point, the third argument is left unchanged, and the function returns zero.

If every character is consumed successfully, the recorded position is discarded, making the consumption permanent. The function then allocates a block of memory large enough to hold the second argument plus a terminating NUL character, copies the second argument into that block, stores the pointer to the copy through the third argument, and returns one.

The second argument must not be NULL and must point to a valid NUL-terminated string. The third argument must not be NULL. The returned copy is owned by the caller and must eventually be released. If allocation fails, the behavior is determined by the allocation helper. No other side effects occur.

The function checks whether the input has reached its end and records that fact in the input state.

The first argument points to the input object whose state is examined and possibly updated. The second argument points to a location that will receive a string pointer; the function always writes NULL through it before doing anything else.

The function first inspects a flag stored in the input state that indicates whether the end of input has already been recorded. If that flag is set, the function returns 0 immediately.

Otherwise, the function calls a helper that determines whether the underlying input source is exhausted. If the helper reports that the input is not exhausted, the function returns 0 and leaves the state flag unchanged.

If the helper reports that the input is exhausted, the function sets the state flag to 1 and returns 1.

Thus the return value is 1 only on the first call that observes the end of input; every subsequent call returns 0, even though the end-of-input flag remains set. The function performs no memory allocation or deallocation, modifies no global data, and has no other side effects beyond writing NULL through the second argument and possibly updating the flag in the first argument’s state.

The function creates and returns a new error object describing a parse failure, or returns NULL when error reporting is suppressed.

The first argument is the input context. The function reads from it the current parse position, the name of the source file, and a flag indicating whether errors should be suppressed. If suppression is enabled, the function returns NULL immediately and performs no other work.

The second argument is a NUL-terminated string describing the failure. It must not be NULL. The function copies this string into the new error object.

When an error object is created, the function allocates memory for the object itself, for a copy of the source file name, and for a copy of the failure description. The file name is taken from the input context and is assumed to be a valid NUL-terminated string. The stored file name and failure description are independent copies; later changes to the original strings do not affect them.

The new error object records the current parse position from the input context, including its row, column, and related state. It sets the count of expected alternatives to zero and stores no list of expected alternatives. It sets the received character to a single space character.

The returned object is newly allocated and owned by the caller. The function does not modify the input context or the failure string.

The function combines several error reports into a single error report. It takes an input context, an array of pointers to error reports, and the number of elements in that array.

The function first scans the array to find the last non-null entry. If every entry is null, it returns null immediately. Otherwise, it allocates a new error report and initializes it with an invalid state, no expected items, no failure message, and a copy of the filename taken from that last non-null entry.

It then scans all non-null entries to find the greatest position among their states, and sets the new report’s state to that state.

Next, it scans the non-null entries again, considering only those whose position equals the greatest position found. For the first such entry that has a failure message, it copies that message into the new report and stops looking at further entries. If an entry at the greatest position has no failure message, the new report takes the received character from that entry and adds each of that entry’s expected items, but only if an identical expected item is not already present in the new report.

Finally, it deletes every non-null entry in the original array and returns the newly created combined report. The returned report owns all memory allocated for it.

The function applies a transformation to a parsed value while managing the input context. It takes three arguments: the first is the input context, the second is a function pointer for the transformation, and the third is the value to transform.

If the transformation function is the one that frees a value, the function instead calls a context-aware freeing routine with the first and third arguments, returning whatever that routine returns. If the transformation function is the one that converts a character into an abstract syntax tree node, the function calls a context-aware conversion routine with the first and third arguments, again returning its result directly.

For any other transformation function, the function first exports the third argument through the input context, producing a pointer suitable for use outside the parser. It then calls the supplied transformation function with that exported pointer as its only argument, and returns whatever the transformation returns.

The function itself performs no error checking on the arguments. It assumes the first argument points to a valid input context and that the third argument is a valid value of the kind expected by the chosen transformation. Ownership of the third argument is transferred to the transformation or to the context-aware routines; the caller must not use it afterward unless the transformation's contract says otherwise. The return value is exactly the result of whichever branch is taken, with no additional modification.

The function grows an array of parse result slots when the parser needs more than the initial stack-provided capacity. The first argument supplies the allocation context used for memory operations. The second argument is the current number of occupied slots, which determines the new capacity. The third argument points to the initial stack-allocated array of results. The fourth argument points to the current results array, which may be the stack array or a previously heap-allocated array.

If the current count equals the minimum stack capacity, the function allocates a new heap array with a capacity one and a half times the current count, copies the existing minimum number of results from the stack array into it, and returns the new array. If the current count is at least the minimum stack capacity, the function reallocates the current array to a capacity one and a half times the current count and returns the resized array. In both cases the existing result values are preserved. The returned pointer is null if allocation fails. The function does not modify the stack array or free the old heap array on failure.

The function attempts to parse input according to a given parser and reports either a successful output or an error.

The first argument is the input source, which must be a valid pointer to an initialized input structure. The second argument is the parser to apply, which must be a valid pointer. The third argument is a pointer to a result union that receives either the parsed output on success or an error description on failure.

The function begins by creating a preliminary error object with the failure message "Unknown Error" and marks its state as invalid. It then runs the parsing process. If parsing succeeds, the preliminary error is discarded, and the result union receives the parsed output after it has been exported to a form suitable for the caller. The function returns 1.

If parsing fails, the preliminary error is merged with whatever error the parsing process produced, the merged error is exported, and the result union receives that exported error. The function returns 0.

The third argument must point to a writable result union. On success, its output member is set; on failure, its error member is set. The returned error or output is owned by the caller and must be released through the appropriate cleanup mechanism. The function does not modify the input source or the parser in an observable way beyond normal parsing side effects.

The function parses an input string using a given parser and returns whether parsing succeeded. The first argument is a filename or label associated with the input, used only for error reporting; it may be NULL. The second argument is the NUL-terminated string to parse; it must not be NULL. The third argument is the parser to apply. The fourth argument points to a result union that receives either the parsed output or an error description.

The function creates a temporary input context from the first two arguments, runs the parser against that context, then destroys the context before returning. The return value is an integer: nonzero indicates the parse succeeded, and zero indicates it failed. On success, the output member of the result union is set to the value produced by the parser; the error member is left untouched. On failure, the error member is set to a newly allocated error structure describing the failure, and the output member is left untouched. The error structure records the filename from the first argument, the position and line/column where parsing stopped, the unexpected character if any, and a list of expected items. Ownership of the error structure passes to the caller, who is responsible for freeing it. The parsed output, if any, is owned according to the parser’s rules. The function itself performs no other side effects and does not modify the input string.

This function opens a file for binary reading and attempts to parse its entire contents using a supplied parser, then closes the file and returns the parsing outcome.

The first argument is a path to the file to be read. It is assumed to be a valid NUL-terminated string. The second argument is a pointer to a parser object that defines the grammar to apply. The third argument is a pointer to a result structure that will receive either the parsed output or an error description.

If the file cannot be opened, the function sets the output member of the result structure to NULL and stores in the error member a newly allocated error object describing the failure to open the file, with the filename and the literal message "Unable to open file!". It then returns 0.

If the file opens successfully, the function delegates parsing to the file-parsing routine, passing the filename, the open file handle, the parser, and the result structure. Whatever that routine returns becomes the return value of this function. The result structure is populated by that routine with either a successful output value or an error object. After parsing completes, the file is closed before the function returns.

The function does not take ownership of the parser or the result structure. Any memory allocated for the error object on failure is the caller's responsibility to release.

Creates a parser that succeeds or fails based on a caller-supplied predicate over two characters, without consuming any input. The first argument is a function pointer taking two character values and returning an integer; it is stored for later use during parsing and is assumed to be a valid, callable function. The function first allocates an uninitialized parser object, then marks it as an anchor-type parser and records the supplied predicate in its anchor-specific data. Finally, it wraps the parser with an expectation label whose literal message is "anchor", and returns the wrapped parser.

The returned parser, when applied to input, invokes the stored predicate with two character arguments determined by the parsing context, and treats a nonzero result as success and zero as failure. It does not advance the input position in either case. The returned object is dynamically allocated and owned by the caller, who is responsible for its eventual release. No other global state is modified. If allocation of the initial parser or the expectation wrapper fails, the behavior follows the underlying allocation and wrapping routines; otherwise the function returns a non-NULL pointer to the newly created parser.

The function creates and returns a new parser that matches any single character from the input. It takes no arguments.

The returned parser is initialized as an undefined parser, then its type is changed to the “any character” kind. Finally, the parser is wrapped with an expectation message so that, when it fails, the recorded error describes the expected input as the literal string “any character”.

The function always returns a non-NULL pointer to a newly allocated parser object. The caller owns this object and is responsible for its eventual release. No other global or external state is modified.

The parser’s observable behavior is: when applied to input, it succeeds if at least one character remains before the end of input, consuming exactly that one character regardless of its value; it fails if the input is empty or already at the end. On failure, the error information associated with the parse includes the expectation message “any character”. No partial input is consumed on failure. The returned parser does not retain or modify the input, and it does not allocate or free memory during parsing.

Creates a parser that recognizes exactly one specific character. The single argument is the character to match; it may be any value representable as a char, including null, newline, or other control characters.

The function first allocates an undefined parser object, then marks it as a single-character parser and stores the given character as the character to match. It then wraps that parser with an expectation message so that, when parsing fails, the reported error names the expected character.

The returned parser, when applied to input, succeeds only if the next character in the input equals the stored character. On success it consumes that one character and returns a pointer to it. On failure it consumes nothing and reports an error whose message is the expected character enclosed in single quotes, for example a single quote, the character, and a closing single quote. If the character itself is a single quote, the message contains that quote between the surrounding quotes.

The returned parser is newly allocated and owned by the caller. No other global or external state is modified. The function does not reject any input value and does not return NULL under normal conditions; allocation failure behavior follows the underlying allocation and undefined-parser construction routines.

Creates a parser that matches any single character contained in a given set. The first argument is a NUL-terminated string listing the allowed characters; it must not be NULL. The function assumes the string is valid and readable.

The returned parser, when applied to input, succeeds if the next input character is one of the characters in that set, consuming exactly one character. If the next character is not in the set, or if there is no input remaining, the parser fails without consuming input.

The function allocates a new parser object and a private copy of the character set string. The copy is owned by the parser and is released when the parser itself is destroyed. The original string passed by the caller is not modified and remains owned by the caller.

The parser is also given an expectation message describing the accepted set. The message is formatted as the literal prefix “one of '”, followed by the original string content, followed by a closing single quote. This message is stored in the parser and is used when reporting parse failures.

If memory allocation for the parser, the string copy, or the expectation message fails, the behavior follows the project’s out-of-memory handling; no partial parser is returned to the caller. On success, the returned parser is fully initialized and ready for use.

Creates a new parser object that wraps an existing parser and transforms its successful result using a caller-supplied function that also receives an extra context value.

The first argument is the parser to be wrapped. It is assumed to be a valid, previously allocated parser object; ownership is not transferred, and the original parser remains unchanged.

The second argument is a function pointer. It must accept two arguments: the result value produced by the wrapped parser, and the context value supplied as the third argument to this function. It returns a new result value, which becomes the result of the new parser.

The third argument is an opaque context value passed unchanged to the transformation function whenever the wrapped parser succeeds. It may be NULL if the transformation function tolerates that.

The function allocates a new parser object of the transformation-with-context kind. It stores the wrapped parser, the transformation function, and the context value inside the new object. The new parser’s name is left unset, and its retained flag is left at its default value.

The return value is a pointer to the newly allocated parser object. The caller owns this object and is responsible for eventually releasing it. If allocation fails, the behavior is undefined. No other side effects occur.

Creates a new parser that succeeds when the parser supplied as the first argument fails, and fails when that parser succeeds. The new parser consumes no input itself.

The first argument is the parser whose result is negated. The second argument is a function used to release any value produced by the first parser when it succeeds but the negation causes overall failure. The third argument is a function used to produce a value when the first parser fails and the negation therefore succeeds.

The function first allocates an uninitialized parser object. If allocation fails, the behavior is undefined. It then marks the new parser as a negation parser and stores the three arguments in its internal state: the wrapped parser, the release function, and the production function.

The returned parser is newly allocated and owned by the caller. It does not take ownership of the first argument; the wrapped parser remains independently valid. The release and production functions are stored as function pointers and are invoked later during parsing, not by this function.

No input is consumed, no global state is modified, and no other side effects occur. The returned parser has no name and is not marked as retained.

Creates a parser that repeatedly applies another parser zero or more times, folding the results into a single value.

The first argument is a fold function that receives the number of parsed results and an array of pointers to those results, and returns a combined value. The second argument is the parser to be repeated.

The function returns a newly allocated parser object. The returned parser has no name and is not marked as retained. Its type is set to the repetition-with-zero-or-more kind. The parser supplied as the second argument is stored inside the returned parser as the sub-parser to repeat, and the fold function supplied as the first argument is stored alongside it.

No parsing occurs during this call. The returned parser is uninitialized except for the fields described above; other fields retain whatever values the underlying allocation produced. The caller owns the returned parser and is responsible for its eventual release. The second argument is not copied or consumed; ownership of it remains with the caller, and the returned parser references it for later use.

Creates a parser that recognizes one or more occurrences of a pattern separated by another pattern. The first argument is a folding function used to combine the results of the matched occurrences into a single value. The second argument is the parser for the separator that must appear between consecutive occurrences. The third argument is the parser for the repeated element.

The function first obtains an uninitialized parser object. It then marks that object as a separator-list parser, stores the element parser, the folding function, and the separator parser inside it, and returns the object.

The returned parser, when applied to input, requires at least one match of the element parser. After the first match, it repeatedly attempts to match the separator parser followed by the element parser. Matching stops when the separator is not found or the element after a separator fails. The folding function receives the number of matched elements and an array of their result values, and its return value becomes the result of the whole parse. The separator results are discarded and not passed to the folding function.

The function itself performs no parsing, allocates no additional memory beyond the parser object, and does not validate the arguments. If the element parser fails on the first attempt, the whole parse fails without invoking the folding function. The returned parser does not retain ownership of the argument parsers; they must remain valid for as long as the returned parser is used.

Creates a parser that attempts to match any one of several alternative parsers, in the order they are supplied. The first argument is the number of alternatives; it must be a non-negative integer. The remaining arguments are that many pointers to parser objects, passed as variadic arguments. The function assumes each such pointer refers to a valid parser.

The returned parser is newly allocated and owned by the caller. Its type is set to the alternative-combinator kind. Internally it stores the count of alternatives and an array of pointers to the supplied parsers, copied in the order given. The returned parser does not take ownership of the alternative parsers; they must remain valid for as long as the returned parser is used.

If the count is zero, the returned parser has no alternatives and will fail on any input. If the count is negative, the behavior is undefined. The function does not check for allocation failure; if memory for the internal array cannot be obtained, the behavior is undefined. No other side effects occur.

This function creates and returns a parser that matches only the start of the input. It takes no arguments.

The returned parser succeeds when it is applied at the very beginning of the input, before any characters have been consumed. If any input has already been consumed, the parser fails. It consumes no input on success.

The parser is constructed by first creating an undefined parser, then setting its type to the special start-of-input type, and finally wrapping it with an expectation message. The expectation message is the literal string "start of input", which is used in error reporting when the parser fails.

The returned parser is dynamically allocated and owned by the caller, who is responsible for eventually releasing it. No other side effects occur. The function always returns a valid parser pointer; it does not return NULL under normal circumstances.

The function decides whether a boundary exists between two adjacent characters in a text buffer. The first argument is the character immediately before the boundary position, and the second argument is the character immediately after it. A boundary is recognized when exactly one side is a word character, where a word character is any ASCII letter, digit, or underscore. The beginning or end of the text is represented by the null character.

The function returns 1 if a boundary is present and 0 otherwise. Specifically, it returns 1 when the second argument is a word character and the first argument is the null character, or when the first argument is a word character and the second argument is the null character. It also returns 1 when the second argument is a word character and the first argument is not, or when the second argument is not a word character and the first argument is. If both arguments are word characters, or neither is, the function returns 0.

The function has no side effects and does not modify its arguments or any global state. It treats all non-word characters, including the null character, punctuation, whitespace, and control characters, as equivalent for the purpose of boundary detection.

This function builds a parser that combines several existing parsers in sequence, folding their results into a single string value. The first argument is the number of parsers to combine. The second argument is an array of that many parser pointers.

The function first creates a base parser that produces an empty string value. It then iterates over the provided parsers in order, each time constructing a new parser that runs the accumulated parser followed by the next provided parser, concatenating their string results. The final accumulated parser is returned.

The returned parser, when applied to input, runs the provided parsers one after another from the beginning of the input. If all succeed, their individual string results are concatenated in the order the parsers were supplied, and that concatenated string is returned as the parse result. If any parser fails, the combined parser fails at that point and no result is produced.

The first argument must be non-negative. If it is zero, the returned parser succeeds without consuming input and yields an empty string. The second argument must point to an array containing at least as many valid parser pointers as the first argument specifies; each parser must produce a string result when it succeeds.

The function allocates new parser structures for the accumulated combination. The original parsers are not modified. The returned parser owns its internal references to the provided parsers and to the intermediate parsers created during construction. No other side effects occur.

The function maps a single escape character to a parser that recognizes the corresponding character class or position in the input. The first argument is the character following a backslash in a regular expression escape sequence.

For the lowercase letters a, f, n, r, t, and v, the returned parser matches the corresponding control character: alert, form feed, newline, carriage return, horizontal tab, and vertical tab, respectively.

For the letter b, the returned parser matches a word boundary without consuming input, and produces an empty string as its result. For the uppercase letter B, the returned parser matches any position that is not a word boundary, also without consuming input, and produces an empty string.

For the uppercase letter A, the returned parser matches only the start of the input, and for the uppercase letter Z, only the end of the input. Both produce an empty string and consume nothing.

For the letter d, the returned parser matches a single decimal digit. For the uppercase letter D, it matches any single character that is not a decimal digit, and produces an empty string as its result.

For the letter s, the returned parser matches a single whitespace character. For the uppercase letter S, it matches any single character that is not whitespace, and produces an empty string.

For the letter w, the returned parser matches a single alphanumeric character or underscore. For the uppercase letter W, it matches any single character that is not alphanumeric or underscore, and produces an empty string.

For any other input character, the function returns NULL.

The function converts a regular-expression character range expression into a parser that matches a single character according to that range. The first argument is a pointer to a NUL-terminated string containing the range expression. The function assumes this pointer is valid and that the string is NUL-terminated.

If the string is empty, or if it consists solely of a leading caret, the function returns a parser that always fails with the message "Invalid Regex Range Expression". In these cases the input string is released.

A leading caret indicates complementation: the resulting parser matches any character not in the specified set. Without a caret, the parser matches any character in the set.

The function processes the remaining characters from left to right. A backslash escapes the next character; if that escaped character has a special translation, the translated text is added to the set, otherwise the character itself is added. A hyphen normally denotes a range from the previous character to the next character, inclusive, and all characters in between are added. A hyphen at the beginning of the expression or at the end is treated as a literal hyphen. Any other character is added literally.

The function releases the input string before returning. The returned parser is newly allocated and owned by the caller.

The function compiles a regular-expression pattern into a parser object. The first argument is a NUL-terminated string containing the pattern; the second argument is an integer mode flag that controls how escaped characters are interpreted during compilation.

The pattern grammar supports grouping with parentheses, character classes with square brackets, alternation with a vertical bar, and the repetition operators star, plus, question mark, and an explicit numeric count enclosed in curly braces. A repetition operator applies to the immediately preceding element. An empty repetition suffix is allowed and leaves the element unchanged. Character classes may contain escaped characters and any characters except a closing square bracket. Outside a class, any character except a vertical bar or closing parenthesis is accepted, and escape sequences are recognized.

The function returns a newly allocated parser object. If the pattern is valid, the returned parser matches the entire input described by the pattern. If the pattern is invalid, the function returns a parser that always fails, and its failure message begins with the literal text “Invalid Regex: ” followed by a description of the syntax error. The returned parser is owned by the caller and must eventually be released. The function does not modify the input string or the mode flag, and it does not retain either after returning.

The function trims trailing whitespace from a NUL-terminated string in place.

The first argument must be a pointer to a modifiable, NUL-terminated character buffer. The function assumes this pointer is valid and that the buffer contains a properly terminated string.

The function scans the string from its end toward the beginning. For every trailing character that is considered whitespace by the standard whitespace classification, it replaces that character with a NUL terminator and continues with the preceding character. It stops at the first character that is not whitespace, or when the beginning of the string is reached.

The return value is the same pointer that was passed in as the first argument, now pointing to the modified string. If the string consists entirely of whitespace, the first character is set to NUL and the returned pointer addresses an empty string. If the string is already empty or has no trailing whitespace, the buffer is unchanged and the same pointer is returned.

The function does not allocate or free memory, does not modify any global state, and does not report errors. The caller retains ownership of the buffer both before and after the call.

The function transforms a string by replacing escape sequences with their literal characters. The first argument must point to a dynamically allocated, NUL-terminated string; ownership of that string passes to this function.

The transformation uses two fixed lookup tables: one lists the escape characters that are recognized, and the other lists the corresponding replacement characters. For each occurrence of a backslash followed by one of the recognized escape characters, the pair is replaced by the matching literal character. Any backslash not followed by a recognized escape character is left unchanged. All other characters are copied through as they are.

The result is a newly allocated, NUL-terminated string. If the input contains no recognized escape sequences, the returned string is still a fresh copy, not the original pointer. The original string is always released before the function returns, regardless of whether any replacements were made.

If memory allocation for the new string fails, the function returns NULL and the original string is still released. No other side effects occur: no globals are modified, no files or streams are touched, and no error indicator is set beyond the allocation failure itself.

The caller owns the returned string and is responsible for releasing it when it is no longer needed.

This function tests whether a parser accepts a given input string and produces an output that satisfies a caller-supplied predicate.

The first argument is a pointer to a parser object. The second argument is a pointer to a NUL-terminated input string to be parsed. The third argument is a pointer to an expected value that will be passed as the second argument to the predicate. The fourth argument is a pointer to a predicate function taking two pointers and returning an integer; it should return nonzero when the parsed output matches the expected value. The fifth argument is a pointer to a cleanup function that releases the parsed output. The sixth argument is ignored entirely.

The function first attempts to parse the input string using the given parser. If parsing fails, the error object produced by the parser is released, and the function returns 1.

If parsing succeeds, the predicate is called with the parsed output as its first argument and the expected value as its second argument. The parsed output is then always released using the cleanup function, regardless of the predicate result. If the predicate returns nonzero, the function returns 0; otherwise it returns 1.

The function has no other side effects. It does not modify the parser, the input string, or the expected value. The cleanup function is called exactly once whenever parsing succeeds, and the error object is released exactly once whenever parsing fails.

This function tests whether a parser accepts a given input string and produces a result matching an expected value.

The first argument is a parser object. The second is a NUL-terminated input string to parse. The third is a pointer to the expected value. The fourth is a comparison callback receiving the parsed output and the expected value, returning nonzero if they match. The fifth is a cleanup callback that releases the parsed output. The sixth is a printing callback that writes a value’s textual representation to standard output.

The function attempts to parse the input. If parsing fails, it prints the parse error, releases the error object, and returns 0.

If parsing succeeds, it calls the comparison callback with the parsed output and expected value. If the callback returns nonzero, the parsed output is passed to the cleanup callback and the function returns 1.

If the comparison returns zero, the function prints “Got ”, prints the parsed output via the printing callback, prints a newline, then prints “Expected ”, prints the expected value, and prints another newline. The parsed output is then cleaned up and the function returns 0.

The function does not modify the parser, input string, or expected value. All arguments and callbacks are assumed valid and non-NULL. The cleanup callback runs exactly once whenever parsing succeeds.

The function creates a new abstract syntax tree node and attaches a caller-specified number of child nodes to it.

The first argument is an integer count of how many child nodes will be supplied. The second argument is a string used as the tag for the newly created node. The remaining arguments are the child nodes themselves, passed as a variable-length list; exactly as many as the count indicates must be provided.

The function begins by creating a new node with the given tag and an empty contents string. It then reads each child node from the variable argument list in order and appends it to the new node’s list of children. The order of children in the resulting node matches the order in which they were passed.

The function returns a pointer to the newly created node, which now owns the supplied child nodes. The caller is responsible for eventually releasing the returned node and its children through the appropriate cleanup mechanism. No validation is performed on the count or on the child pointers; if the count is negative or exceeds the number of arguments actually supplied, the behavior is undefined. If the count is zero, the returned node has no children. The tag string is copied or otherwise retained by the node according to the node-creation behavior, and the function does not modify the child nodes themselves.

The function appends a child node to a parent syntax-tree node. The first argument is a pointer to the parent structure, which must not be NULL and must have been initialized with a valid child array and child count. The second argument is a pointer to the child structure to append; it may be NULL, in which case a NULL pointer is stored as the new child.

The function increments the parent's child count by one, then grows the parent's dynamic array of child pointers to hold the new count. If reallocation fails, the standard out-of-memory behavior of the C library applies: the function does not return, and the parent's child count has already been incremented, leaving the structure in an inconsistent state. If reallocation succeeds, the new child pointer is stored in the last slot of the enlarged array.

The function returns the first argument unchanged, regardless of whether the appended child pointer is NULL. The parent takes ownership of the child pointer in the sense that the child becomes part of the parent's child list; the function itself does not copy or free the child. No other fields of the parent or child are modified. The order of operations is: increment the count, reallocate the array, then assign the new child to the final position.

The function prepends a tag to the tag string stored inside the structure pointed to by the first argument. If the first argument is NULL, it returns NULL immediately without any other effect.

The first argument must point to a valid structure whose tag member is either NULL or a NUL-terminated string. The second argument must point to a NUL-terminated string that is not NULL.

The function allocates enough memory to hold the new tag, which consists of the second argument’s string, followed by a vertical bar character, followed by the existing tag string. If the existing tag is NULL, it is treated as an empty string. The new tag is stored back into the structure’s tag member, replacing the old pointer. The old tag memory is released or reused by the allocation routine as appropriate.

The function returns the first argument unchanged, now with its tag member updated. If memory allocation fails, the behavior follows the allocation routine’s failure semantics; the function does not check for allocation failure itself.

The contents, state, and children of the structure are not modified. No other memory is allocated or freed, and no global state is changed.

The function modifies the abstract syntax tree node passed as the first argument by prepending a prefix to its tag string. The second argument is a NUL-terminated string whose final character is treated as a delimiter and is not copied; only the characters before that final character are inserted at the beginning of the existing tag.

If the first argument is NULL, the function returns NULL immediately without any other effect. Otherwise, the node’s tag must already be a valid heap-allocated string. The function reallocates that string to hold the combined length of the prefix and the original tag plus a terminating NUL byte. The original tag bytes, including the terminator, are shifted right to make room, and the prefix characters are copied into the front. The resulting tag is therefore the prefix followed immediately by the original tag, with no separator added.

The function returns the first argument unchanged as a pointer. It does not allocate or free the node itself, does not modify any other member of the node, and does not alter the second argument. If memory allocation for the enlarged tag fails, the behavior follows the standard allocation failure rules for the allocation function used. No other error conditions are reported.

Creates a parser that attempts to match input using one of several alternative sub-parsers, in the order they are supplied.

The first argument is an integer specifying how many alternative parsers follow. It must be non-negative. The remaining arguments are that many pointers to existing parser objects; each is used as one alternative. The function does not copy or take ownership of those parsers, but stores their pointers.

The function returns a pointer to a newly allocated parser object. The returned parser has its kind set to the alternative-choice type. Its stored count equals the first argument, and it holds a dynamically allocated array of exactly that many parser pointers, filled in the order the arguments were passed. If the first argument is zero, the array allocation may still occur with size zero, and the returned parser contains no alternatives.

The function does not check any argument for validity. If memory allocation for the array fails, the behavior is undefined. The returned parser is newly allocated and owned by the caller, who is responsible for eventually freeing it. The alternative parsers referenced by the returned parser are not freed or modified by this function. No global state is changed.

The function builds a parser that succeeds only when all of a given set of parsers succeed in sequence. It takes two arguments: the first is a count, and the second is a pointer to an array of parser pointers of that length.

It begins with a parser that always succeeds without consuming input. It then walks through the array in order. For each element that is not NULL, it combines the accumulated parser with that element using a two-parser sequencing operation, so the accumulated result must match first and then the current element must match. NULL elements are skipped and do not affect the result.

The return value is a pointer to the final combined parser. If the count is zero, or if every element in the array is NULL, the returned parser is the initial always-succeeding parser. If exactly one element is non-NULL, the returned parser is a sequence of the always-succeeding parser followed by that element, which behaves like that element alone. If more than one element is non-NULL, the returned parser requires all of them to match in the order they appear in the array, ignoring any NULL entries.

The function does not modify the input array or the parsers it contains. It does not free any memory. The returned parser is newly allocated by the sequencing operation and is owned by the caller. No error conditions are reported; NULL array elements are simply ignored.

The function converts a parsed string token into a tagged parser state for a grammar definition.

The first argument is a pointer to a value that must be a string produced by an earlier parsing step; it is assumed to be non-NULL and to contain a valid, NUL-terminated character sequence. The second argument is a pointer to a grammar state structure; it is assumed to be non-NULL and to contain a flags field whose bits encode language options.

The function first unescapes the input string, producing a new dynamically allocated string in which escape sequences are replaced by their literal characters. The original input is not modified. The unescaped string is then used to build a parser that matches exactly that literal character sequence. If the whitespace-sensitive flag is set in the grammar state, the parser is used directly; otherwise the parser is wrapped so that it also consumes surrounding whitespace as defined by the grammar’s tokenization rules.

The temporary unescaped string is released before the function returns. The resulting parser is then transformed so that when it succeeds it produces an abstract syntax tree node containing the matched string, and that node is tagged with the literal tag “string”. Finally, the parser is wrapped to carry parser state, and the resulting parser pointer is returned.

The function always returns a non-NULL parser pointer. It does not modify the grammar state structure. Memory for the returned parser and any internal structures is allocated by the helper functions and remains owned by the caller. If allocation fails inside any helper, the behavior follows that helper’s error handling.

The function converts a grammar rule for a single character into a parser that recognizes that character and produces an abstract syntax tree node tagged as a character literal.

The first argument is a pointer to a value representing an escaped character string. It is assumed to be non-NULL and to contain at least one character after unescaping. The second argument points to a grammar state structure whose flags field is read to determine whether whitespace is significant.

The function first unescapes the input string, producing a newly allocated string. The first character of that unescaped string is used to build a parser that matches exactly that character. If the whitespace-sensitive flag is set in the grammar state, the parser matches the character directly; otherwise, the parser is wrapped so that surrounding whitespace is skipped before and after the character.

The unescaped string is then freed. The character parser is transformed so that when it succeeds, it yields an abstract syntax tree node containing the matched character as a string. That parser is then tagged with the literal tag "char" and wrapped so that it records parser state information.

The return value is the resulting parser object. On failure to allocate memory at any stage, the function returns NULL. The input value is not modified, and ownership of it remains with the caller. The returned parser owns any memory it allocates internally.

The function builds a regular-expression parser from three arguments supplied in an array. The first argument is a string containing the regular expression pattern. The second argument is a string of mode flags. The third argument points to a grammar state structure whose flags field controls whitespace handling.

The function ignores the integer argument. It examines the second argument for the characters 'm' and 's'. If 'm' is present, it enables multiline mode; if 's' is present, it enables dot-all mode. These modes are combined with a default mode value.

The first argument is passed through a helper that unescapes regular-expression syntax, producing a newly allocated string. That unescaped string is then used to create a regular-expression parser with the computed mode flags. If the grammar state indicates that whitespace is significant, the parser is used directly; otherwise, the parser is wrapped so that surrounding whitespace is skipped automatically.

The unescaped string and the mode-flag string are both freed after the parser is created. The resulting parser is then transformed by applying a string-to-AST conversion function, tagged with the literal tag "regex", and finally converted into a stateful parser, which is returned. The returned parser is newly allocated and owned by the caller.

The function resolves a textual reference to a parser using a state object that holds a variable-argument list, a count of collected parsers, and a dynamically allocated array of parser pointers.

The first argument is a NUL-terminated string. If it consists entirely of a decimal integer, it is treated as a positional index. The function converts it to an integer and ensures the collected array has at least that many entries plus one. It extends the array by reading additional parser pointers from the variable-argument list, incrementing the count each time. If a newly read pointer is NULL, it returns a failure value whose message states the requested position and the number of parsers actually supplied. Otherwise it returns the parser at the requested position.

If the first argument is not a number, it is treated as a name. The function first scans the parsers already collected. If it encounters a NULL entry, it returns a failure value reporting the name as unknown. If it finds a parser whose stored name matches the string exactly, it returns that parser. If no match is found, it repeatedly reads further parser pointers from the variable-argument list, appending each to the collected array and incrementing the count. If a read pointer is NULL or has no stored name, it returns a failure value reporting the name as unknown. If a read parser’s stored name matches the string, it returns that parser.

The function may allocate or reallocate memory for the collected array. On failure paths it returns a failure value and leaves the array extended with any entries read before the failure.

This function resolves a grammar identifier reference during grammar construction. The first argument is a pointer to a string naming a parser defined earlier in the grammar; the second argument points to the state accumulated while building the grammar.

The function first locates the parser associated with the given name by searching the grammar state. It then releases the memory used by the name string, since the name is no longer needed after lookup.

If the located parser has a non-empty name, the function attaches that name as a tag to the parser, wraps the result as the grammar root, and then wraps that root as a state object, returning the final pointer. If the located parser has no name, the function skips the tagging step and returns the state-wrapped root of the parser directly.

The return value is always a pointer to a state object wrapping the root parser. The function assumes the first argument is a valid, heap-allocated, NUL-terminated string and that the second argument points to a valid grammar state containing the named parser. If the name is not found, behavior is undefined. The only side effect is freeing the input string; the located parser and grammar state are not freed. The returned object is newly created and owned by the caller.

The function compiles a grammar specification given as a NUL-terminated string into a parser object. The second argument points to a structure that carries compilation state, including a set of flags and a list of parsers accumulated during compilation.

The first argument must be a valid NUL-terminated string containing the grammar text. The second argument must point to a valid, initialized state structure; it is not modified except through the normal compilation side effects of the grammar actions.

The grammar text is parsed according to a fixed grammar of rules, terms, factors, and bases. It accepts string literals, character literals, regular expressions with optional case-insensitivity or multiline flags, identifiers, parenthesized subexpressions, and repetition suffixes such as star, plus, question mark, exclamation mark, or a bracketed integer count. Whitespace is skipped around tokens.

If the input parses completely, the function returns the resulting parser object. If parsing fails, the function returns a parser object that always fails, whose failure message begins with the literal text “Invalid Grammar: ” followed by a human-readable description of the parse error. In that case, any partially constructed parser objects from the failed parse are discarded.

Before returning, the function optimizes the resulting parser. If the state structure’s flags include the predictive-language bit, the returned parser is wrapped to make it predictive; otherwise it is returned as built. The returned parser is newly allocated and owned by the caller.

The function constructs a statement record from an array of six parsed values. It allocates a new structure of the statement type and fills three of its members: the first member receives the first argument, the second member receives the second argument, and the third member receives the fourth argument. The first two arguments are expected to be strings, and the fourth argument is expected to be a pointer to a parser structure. The function does not validate these arguments.

The third and fifth arguments are expected to be strings that are no longer needed; the function releases the memory they point to. The first, second, and fourth arguments are not freed and their ownership is transferred into the newly allocated structure. The sixth argument is ignored entirely, as is the integer first parameter, which is not used.

The function returns a pointer to the newly allocated statement structure. If allocation fails, the standard allocation function returns NULL, and the function returns NULL without freeing any of the input arguments. The function has no other side effects and does not modify any global state.

The function accepts a count and an array of pointers to statement structures, and produces a newly allocated array of pointers that contains the same pointers in the same order, followed by a NULL sentinel. The first argument specifies how many pointers are present in the second argument. The second argument is assumed to point to at least that many valid pointer elements; it is not modified.

The function allocates memory for an array of pointers with one extra slot beyond the given count. If allocation fails, the function returns NULL. Otherwise, it copies each pointer from the input array into the corresponding position of the new array, then stores NULL in the final slot. The returned array therefore has one more element than the count, and the last element is always NULL.

The function does not copy or inspect the pointed-to statement structures themselves, and it does not release any memory. Ownership of the original pointers is unchanged; the caller retains responsibility for them. Ownership of the newly allocated array passes to the caller, who must eventually free it. The function has no other side effects and does not modify any global state.

The function parses a complete grammar description from the input source provided as the first argument, using the grammar state supplied as the second argument to build and register the resulting grammar rules.

The first argument is an input object that provides the text to parse and tracks parsing state. The second argument is a grammar state object that accumulates the parsed rules and any associated data.

The grammar description consists of one or more statements. Each statement has an identifier, an optional string literal, a colon, a grammar expression, and a semicolon. Whitespace is allowed around tokens. The grammar expression supports alternation separated by vertical bars, sequences of one or more repetition units, and repetition suffixes: an asterisk, plus, question mark, exclamation mark, or a bracketed integer. A repetition unit may be a string literal, a character literal, a regular expression literal optionally followed by one or more of the letters m or s, an identifier or digit sequence enclosed in braces, or a parenthesized grammar expression.

On successful parsing of the entire input, the function returns NULL and the second argument is updated with the parsed grammar rules. On failure, it returns a pointer to an error object describing the parse failure, including the expected inputs, the received character, and the position in the input. The second argument is not updated on failure. The function always releases the temporary parser objects it creates before returning.

This function parses a grammar specification supplied as a string and, through a variable argument list, associates named rules with parser objects provided by the caller.

The first argument is a set of bit flags that control parsing behavior. The second argument is a NUL-terminated string containing the grammar definition. It must not be NULL. The remaining arguments are variable in number and type; they are consumed according to the grammar rules encountered during parsing. Each such argument is expected to be a pointer to a parser object that will be assigned to the corresponding named rule in the grammar.

The function returns a pointer to an error structure. If parsing succeeds, the return value is NULL. If parsing fails, the return value points to a newly allocated error structure describing the failure, including the position, expected inputs, and the actual input received. The caller is responsible for freeing this error structure.

The function creates an internal input source from the grammar string, with a fixed internal filename. It then invokes the core grammar parser, passing the flags, the variable argument list, and an initially empty collection of parser assignments. After parsing, the internal input source is destroyed and any temporary storage for parser assignments is released. The variable argument list is ended before returning.

The function has no other side effects on global state. It does not modify the grammar string. Memory for the returned error structure, if any, is allocated and owned by the caller.

The function checks whether a byte sequence is valid UTF-8 text. The first argument points to the beginning of the bytes to examine, and the second argument gives the number of bytes to examine. The first argument must not be NULL when the second argument is greater than zero.

The function processes the input from beginning to end, validating one encoded character at a time. For each position, it asks a helper routine to validate the encoded character starting there and to report how many bytes that character occupies. If the helper reports failure for any position, the function immediately returns the integer value 0. If every byte from the start to the end is consumed by a sequence of valid encoded characters, the function returns the integer value 1.

An empty input, indicated by a second argument of zero, is considered valid and yields the integer value 1. The function does not modify the input bytes, does not allocate or release memory, and has no other side effects. It does not record error details; the only observable outcomes are the two integer return values. If an invalid sequence is found, validation stops at the first such sequence, and no information about how many bytes were successfully validated before the failure is returned.

The function creates and returns a new empty object value. It takes one argument: a pointer to the value that will wrap the new object. The caller must provide a valid pointer; the function does not check it for NULL.

The function first allocates memory for the object structure using the project’s configured allocation function. If allocation fails, it returns NULL immediately. Otherwise, it stores the supplied wrapping pointer inside the new structure and initializes the object with an initial capacity of zero. If initialization fails, the allocated structure is released using the project’s configured deallocation function and the function returns NULL.

On success, the returned pointer refers to a fully initialized, empty object with no members. The object holds a reference to the wrapping value passed in as the first argument; ownership of that wrapping value is not transferred or released by this function. The returned object itself is newly allocated and becomes the caller’s responsibility to release through the appropriate deallocation mechanism. No other globals or side effects are modified. The function reports failure only by returning NULL; it does not record any error state elsewhere.

Initializes an object structure for storing key–value pairs. The first argument points to the structure to initialize; the second argument is the requested initial capacity for the internal lookup table.

The function first clears all internal pointers and counters in the structure, then records the requested table capacity and derives a smaller item capacity as seven tenths of that value, rounded down. If the requested capacity is zero, the structure is left with null pointers and zero counts, and success is returned.

For a nonzero capacity, the function attempts to allocate five internal arrays: one for the lookup table itself, sized to the requested capacity, and four for names, values, index links, and hash values, each sized to the derived item capacity. If any allocation fails, all arrays allocated so far are released, the structure’s pointers are left null, its counts remain zero, and failure is returned. If all allocations succeed, every entry of the lookup table is set to the invalid index value, and success is returned.

The function does not initialize or allocate the individual name strings or value objects; it only prepares the containers. On failure, no partial arrays remain allocated. The caller retains ownership of the structure passed in.

The function locates the storage slot for a key in a hash table that backs a JSON object. The first argument points to the object structure; the second is a pointer to the key bytes; the third is the length of that key; the fourth is a precomputed hash of the key; the fifth points to a boolean flag that receives whether the key was found.

The function assumes the object is valid, its cell table has a power-of-two capacity, the key pointer is valid for at least the given length, and the output flag pointer is not NULL. It first clears the output flag to false.

It probes the cell table starting at the index derived from the hash, advancing linearly with wraparound, for at most the table capacity. At each probed slot, if the slot is empty, it returns that slot index and leaves the flag false. If the slot is occupied, it compares the stored hash with the supplied hash; on mismatch it continues probing. On hash match, it compares the stored key’s length and bytes with the supplied key. If they match, it sets the output flag to true and returns the slot index. If the key does not match, probing continues.

If the entire table is probed without finding the key or an empty slot, it returns the invalid-index sentinel value, the maximum value of the size type, and leaves the flag false. The function does not modify the object or allocate memory.

The function adds a new key–value pair to a JSON object. The first argument is the target object, the second is the key string, and the third is the value to associate with that key. All three must be non-NULL; otherwise the function returns the failure status immediately and modifies nothing.

The key string is assumed to be NUL-terminated. The function takes ownership of both the key string and the value: on success they become part of the object and must not be freed separately by the caller. The key must not already exist in the object; if it does, the function returns the failure status without changing the object.

If the object has no room for another entry, the function first attempts to grow its internal storage and rehash existing entries. If that allocation or rehashing fails, the function returns the failure status and leaves the object unchanged.

On success, the function stores the key and value as a new entry, records the hash and storage position for later lookup, increments the entry count, and sets the parent link of the added value to the wrapper value associated with the object. It then returns the success status. The order of internal updates is not observable except through the final state of the object.

The function removes a member from a nested object using a dot-separated path. The first argument is a pointer to the object from which removal starts. The second argument is a NUL-terminated string containing the path to the target member; path components are separated by a single period character. The third argument is a boolean flag indicating whether the value being removed should also be deallocated.

If the path contains no period, the function delegates to the helper that removes a direct member from the given object, passing all three arguments unchanged, and returns that helper's result.

If the path contains at least one period, the function locates the first period. It treats the substring before that period as the name of a direct member of the given object and looks it up using a length-limited lookup. If the member does not exist, or if it exists but its value is not an object, the function returns the failure status without modifying anything.

If the named member exists and holds an object, the function calls itself recursively on that nested object, using the remainder of the path after the first period as the new path, and the same deallocation flag. The result of the recursive call is returned directly.

The function performs no allocation and does not modify the path string. It may deallocate the removed value only when the flag is true and a removal actually occurs. If any intermediate component is missing or is not an object, no removal happens and the failure status is returned.

The function creates and initializes a new array container. It takes one argument: a pointer to a value object that will wrap, or own, the new array. The function assumes this pointer is valid; it does not check it.

The function first attempts to allocate memory for the array container using the project’s configured allocation function. If allocation fails, it returns NULL and does not modify anything else.

On success, the function returns a pointer to the newly allocated array container. The container is initialized so that its wrapping value is set to the first argument, its internal item storage is NULL, and both its item count and its storage capacity are zero. No items are allocated or copied, and no other objects or global state are modified.

The returned container is empty and owns no item storage at this point. The caller is responsible for later releasing the container and any items added to it through the appropriate project functions. The first argument is not retained beyond being stored as the wrapping value; ownership of that value is not transferred or duplicated by this function.

The function appends a value to a dynamic array of values. The first argument points to the array that receives the new element; the second argument points to the value to append. The second argument must not be NULL.

Before inserting, the function checks whether the array has room for one more element. If it is full, it attempts to grow the backing storage. The new size is twice the current capacity, unless that would be less than a fixed minimum of 16 elements, in which case the minimum is used. If the growth operation fails, the function returns the failure status, the array is left unchanged, and the second argument is not inserted.

On success, the function records the array as the parent of the appended value, stores the value as the last element of the array, and increments the array's element count by one. The array takes ownership of the value in the sense that the value is now reachable through the array and its parent link points back to the array. The function then returns the success status.

The function does not copy the value; it stores the pointer exactly as given. It does not modify the contents of the value other than setting its parent link. If the array already has enough capacity, no allocation or reallocation occurs. The order of observable changes on success is: the parent link is set first, then the element is stored, then the count is increased.

The function changes the storage capacity of the array structure pointed to by the first argument to the value given by the second argument. The first argument must point to a valid array structure. The second argument is the requested number of element slots; it must be greater than zero.

If the requested capacity is zero, the function returns the failure status and leaves the array unchanged. Otherwise, it attempts to allocate a new block of memory large enough to hold that many pointers to value structures. If allocation fails, it returns the failure status and leaves the array unchanged.

On success, any existing elements are copied into the new storage, preserving their order. The number of elements currently in the array is not changed. The old storage is released. The array’s internal pointer is updated to the new storage, and its recorded capacity is set to the requested value. The function then returns the success status.

The function does not modify the elements themselves, only the container that holds their pointers. It does not change the parent linkage of any element. If the array currently has no elements, no copying occurs, but the old storage, if any, is still released. The new storage is owned by the array and will be released when the array is destroyed or resized again.

The function advances a parser over a quoted string in a NUL-terminated character sequence. The first argument is a pointer to a pointer to the current character; it must not be NULL, and the pointed-to pointer must reference a valid character sequence.

The function first checks that the current character is a double quote. If it is not, the function returns the failure status without advancing the pointer. Otherwise it advances past the opening quote and scans forward until it finds the closing double quote. Within the string, a backslash escapes the next character, so the function skips both the backslash and the character that follows it, whatever that character is. If the end of the sequence is reached before a closing quote is found, the function returns the failure status. This includes the case where a backslash is the final character before the terminator.

On success, the function advances the pointer past the closing quote and returns the success status. On failure, the pointer is left at whatever position the scan had reached: either the original position when the first character was not a quote, or the position where the missing closing quote or escaped character was expected. The function does not allocate or release memory, does not modify the characters themselves, and has no other side effects.
