If the loop ends without an earlier return, the saved offset is restored and the function returns false. The offset is modified only on successful matches or by delegated helpers; on failure it is reset to its original value.

The function allocates and initializes a new expression node. The first argument is an integer type code that determines the node’s category and, for callable nodes, how many parameter slots it has. The second argument is an optional pointer to an array of pointers that supply the initial parameter values.

The allocation size is computed from the type code: the base node size plus space for the declared number of parameter pointers, plus one extra pointer slot when the type code marks the node as a closure. If allocation fails, the function returns NULL.

On success, the entire allocated block is zeroed. If the node has a nonzero number of parameter slots and the second argument is not NULL, the parameter pointer array is copied into the node’s parameter area. The type code is then stored in the node’s first field, and the node is returned.

The function does not validate the type code, does not check whether the second argument contains enough pointers, and does not retain or release ownership of the pointed-to parameter objects. The caller owns the returned allocation and is responsible for freeing it. No other globals or side effects are modified.

The function creates a node representing a callable operation, taking ownership of two child expression nodes. The first argument is an integer type value that encodes the operation category and, for function or closure categories, the number of parameters. The second argument is a pointer to the callable implementation to be stored in the new node. The third and fourth arguments are pointers to child expression nodes; the fourth is used only when the operation requires two parameters.

If the third argument is null, or if the operation requires two parameters and the fourth argument is null, the function fails. On failure, it releases both child nodes if they are non-null and returns null. Otherwise, it attempts to allocate a new node of the given type with the supplied children. If allocation fails, it likewise releases both children and returns null.

On success, the returned node has the given type, owns the supplied children, and stores the callable pointer in its function member. The caller must not free the children after a successful call. The function performs no other side effects and does not modify the children.

The function computes the factorial of a non-negative real number given as its only argument, returning the result as a double-precision floating-point value.

The argument is first checked for validity. If it is not a non-negative number, including the case where it is the floating-point not-a-number value, the function returns the floating-point not-a-number value. If the argument exceeds the largest value representable by an unsigned integer type, the function returns positive infinity.

Otherwise, the fractional part of the argument is discarded by converting it to an unsigned integer. The factorial is then computed by multiplying the integers from one up to that converted value, inclusive. If at any step the multiplication would exceed the largest value representable by an unsigned long long integer type, the function immediately returns positive infinity without completing the remaining multiplications.

If the computation completes without overflow, the exact integer factorial is converted to a double-precision floating-point value and returned. For an argument of zero, the result is one. The function performs no input or output, allocates no memory, and modifies no external state.

The function computes the greatest common divisor of two nonnegative integers supplied as its first and second arguments. It returns the largest integer that divides both inputs without remainder. If either input is zero, the result is the other input; if both are zero, the result is zero. The computation is exact for all values representable in the unsigned 64-bit integer type, including the maximum possible value. No error conditions exist, and no inputs are rejected. The function performs no input or output, allocates no memory, and modifies no global or caller-visible state. It has no side effects. The arguments are passed by value, so the caller’s copies are unchanged. The result is returned directly as an unsigned 64-bit integer. The function is deterministic: for the same pair of inputs it always returns the same value. The order of the two arguments does not affect the result.

The function computes the binomial coefficient for two non-negative real arguments, treating them as counts of total items and chosen items. If either argument is not a non-negative number, or if the first is smaller than the second, the result is the floating-point not-a-number value. If either argument exceeds the largest value representable by an unsigned 32-bit integer, the result is positive infinity.

Otherwise, both arguments are converted to unsigned 64-bit integers. The second argument is reduced by symmetry so that it is no larger than half of the first, minimizing the number of multiplication steps. The computation proceeds iteratively, maintaining an exact integer result at every step. Before each multiplication, the current result and the loop divisor are reduced by their greatest common divisor to prevent intermediate overflow where possible. If at any point the next multiplication would exceed the maximum value of an unsigned 64-bit integer, the function immediately returns positive infinity.

If no overflow occurs, the function returns the exact binomial coefficient as a double-precision floating-point value. The function has no side effects: it does not modify any external state, allocate memory, or write to any object. It only reads its two arguments and returns a value.

The function searches a fixed, sorted table of built-in entries for one whose name matches a caller-supplied prefix. The first argument points to the beginning of a text string to compare; the second argument gives the number of characters from that string to use in the comparison. The first argument is assumed to point to at least that many readable characters.

The search uses binary search over the table, excluding the final sentinel entry. Comparison is performed lexicographically against each table entry’s name, considering only the given prefix length. If the prefix matches exactly, the comparison then checks the next character of the table entry’s name against the null terminator, so that a table name that is longer than the prefix sorts after the prefix, while an exact-length match sorts equal.

If an entry is found whose name equals the given prefix exactly, the function returns a pointer to that table entry. If no such entry exists, it returns NULL. The function does not modify the input string, the table, or any global state, and it does not allocate or release memory. The returned pointer, when non-NULL, refers to an element of the fixed table and remains valid for the lifetime of the program.

The function searches a table of named entries for one whose name matches a given string prefix of a specified length, requiring that the entry’s full name ends exactly at that length.

The first argument points to a structure that holds, among other things, a pointer to an array of entries and a count of how many entries that array contains. The second argument points to the first character of the name to look up. The third argument gives the number of characters to compare.

The function walks through the array from the first entry to the last. For each entry, it compares the first characters of the entry’s name with the supplied name, up to the given length. If those characters are equal and the entry’s name has its terminating null character immediately after that many characters, the entry is considered a match.

If a matching entry is found, the function returns a pointer to that entry within the array. If the array pointer is null, the array count is zero, or no entry satisfies the match condition, the function returns a null pointer.

The function does not modify any memory, does not allocate or release resources, and has no side effects. It only reads the supplied name, the array, and the names stored in the array entries. The comparison is case-sensitive and stops after the given length or at the first difference, whichever comes first.

Parses a numeric literal from the text at the current position of the state structure pointed to by the first argument. The literal may be a hexadecimal constant beginning with zero followed by x or X and at least one hexadecimal digit, or a decimal constant with optional fractional part and optional exponent. Parsing is independent of the current locale.

The function assumes the current position points into a valid string. It examines characters starting there and consumes the longest prefix that forms a valid number. For hexadecimal input, it consumes all consecutive hexadecimal digits after the prefix and computes the integer value. For decimal input, it consumes leading digits, then an optional decimal point followed by digits, then an optional exponent marker e or E, an optional sign, and one or more digits. A lone decimal point with no digits on either side is not a number. If an exponent marker is present but not followed by digits, the marker and any sign are not consumed, so the number ends before them.

The returned value is the parsed number as a double. The current position in the state structure is advanced past the consumed characters, and the type member is set to the numeric-token indicator. If the input is a lone decimal point, the type member is set to the error indicator and zero is returned; the current position is not advanced in that case. No other side effects occur.

The function records that the parser has recognized an operator written between its operands. It updates the state structure pointed to by the first argument in three ways. First, it sets the token-type member to the value that identifies this kind of operator token. Second, it stores the second argument, a pointer to the operator’s implementation function, in the member that holds a function pointer. Third, it stores the third argument, an integer precedence level, in the member that holds the current precedence.

The function does not validate its arguments. The first argument must point to a valid, writable state structure. The second argument may be any pointer value and is stored unchanged. The third argument may be any integer and is stored unchanged.

The function returns no value. It performs no memory allocation or deallocation, does not modify any global or external state, and does not read or write through the stored function pointer. It only modifies the three members of the structure pointed to by the first argument. The order of those modifications is: token type first, then function pointer, then precedence. No other members of the structure are changed.

The function compares the character supplied as the second argument with the character currently pointed to by the first member of the structure passed as the first argument. If they differ, it returns zero and leaves the structure unchanged. If they match, it advances that first member by one character position and returns one.

The first argument must point to a valid structure whose first member points to a valid, readable character. The second argument is the character to test. The function performs no allocation, releases no memory, and modifies no global state. The only possible side effect is the advancement of the first member of the structure, and this occurs only when the comparison succeeds. The return value is exactly zero for a mismatch and exactly one for a match.

Advances the lexer state to the next token in the input string. The first argument points to a structure holding the current input position and receiving the token description; it must be valid, and its input pointer must be valid.

The function first clears the token type and precedence, then repeatedly examines the current input character until a token is produced or input ends. At end of input it records the end-of-input token and returns.

If the current character is a digit or period, it calls the number parser, which consumes the numeric literal and stores its value.

If the current character is a letter, it consumes a run of letters, digits, and underscores. It searches first the caller-supplied lookup table, then the built-in table, for a matching name. If none is found, it records an error token. If the entry denotes a variable, it records a variable token and stores the entry’s address as the bound value. If the entry denotes a function or closure, it records the entry’s type, stores its address as the function pointer, and for closures stores the entry’s context. If the entry’s type is unrecognized, it records an error token.

Otherwise it consumes one character. Single-character operators set the token type, function pointer, and precedence. Two-character operators require the second character to match exactly; otherwise an error token is recorded. Parentheses and comma produce their respective tokens; comma also sets a function pointer and list precedence. Whitespace is skipped. Any other character produces an error token.

The function parses the next syntactic unit of an expression from the token stream held in the structure pointed to by its single argument, and returns a newly allocated expression node.

If the current token is a numeric literal, the function creates a constant node, stores the token’s numeric value, and advances. If it is a variable reference, the function creates a variable node, stores the token’s bound-variable pointer, and advances.

If the token denotes a callable of zero through seven parameters, the function creates a node of the corresponding kind, stores the token’s function pointer, and, for closures, also stores the token’s context pointer as an extra trailing parameter. It then advances. For one parameter, the argument is parsed as a power-level expression and stored as the first parameter. For two or more parameters, an opening parenthesis must follow; the function consumes it, then parses each argument as a logical-or-level expression, separated by commas, until the declared count is reached. A closing parenthesis must then follow. If the separators, argument count, or closing parenthesis are wrong, the current token is set to the error token, but the node is still returned. For zero parameters, parentheses are optional; if present, an empty pair is consumed. For one or more parameters, a missing opening parenthesis sets the error token.

If the current token is an opening parenthesis, the function consumes it, parses a list-level expression, and requires a closing parenthesis afterward; otherwise it sets the error token.

For any other token, the function creates a node of type zero, sets the current token to the error token, and stores the not-a-number value in the node.

If any allocation fails, the function returns NULL. On success it returns the new node.

The function parses a unary power expression from the current token stream. It consumes any leading prefix operators among addition, subtraction, and logical negation, tracking both an overall numeric sign and whether logical negation is applied. A subtraction sign is ignored if logical negation has already been seen, since negating after logical inversion is redundant. Logical negation toggles between one and two applications.

After consuming the prefix operators, the function checks whether the current nesting depth has reached the maximum allowed. If so, it marks the token stream as being in an error state and returns a null pointer without consuming further input. Otherwise it increments the depth, parses a base expression by calling the base parser, and decrements the depth.

If any prefix operator was applied, the parsed base expression is wrapped in a new unary function node representing the combined effect of the sign and logical operations. The wrapper is marked as pure. The function records whether a unary wrapper was created in a state flag used by the exponentiation parser to distinguish an explicit leading sign from a parenthesized negative number. This flag is set only after the base expression has been parsed, so nested parsing cannot overwrite it.

The function returns the resulting expression node, or a null pointer if the depth limit was exceeded.

Parses one precedence level of left-associative binary operators from the token stream held in the structure pointed to by the first argument. The second argument is the precedence level to parse.

The function first parses a single operand at the given precedence level by delegating to the operand parser. If that parser fails and returns a null pointer, the function returns a null pointer immediately.

It then repeatedly examines the current token. The loop continues only while the current token is either a binary operator token or a separator token, and its precedence exactly matches the requested level. For each such token, the function records the operator’s implementation pointer, advances to the next token, parses the right-hand operand at the same precedence level, and combines the accumulated left expression with that right operand into a new two-argument function node marked as pure. If the right operand parser fails, the function returns a null pointer. If allocation of a combined node fails, it also returns a null pointer.

The return value is a pointer to the parsed expression tree for that precedence level, or a null pointer on any failure. The function does not modify global state; it only advances the token stream and allocates new expression nodes. Ownership of the returned tree passes to the caller.

The function evaluates an expression tree node and returns its numeric result as a double.

If the first argument is NULL, the function returns NaN.

Otherwise, the function examines the type of the node, which is stored in its first member. The type is masked to isolate the low five bits, and the result determines the behavior.

If the masked type indicates a constant, the function returns the numeric value stored in the node’s second member.

If the masked type indicates a variable, the function returns the value pointed to by the node’s second member, which is treated as a pointer to a double.

If the masked type indicates a function of zero through seven arguments, the function evaluates each child node, if any, by calling itself recursively on the corresponding entries of the node’s parameter array. It then calls the function pointer stored in the node’s second member, passing the evaluated child results as arguments in order. The return value of that call is returned.

If the masked type indicates a closure of zero through seven arguments, the function behaves similarly, but the first argument to the stored function pointer is the pointer stored in the first entry of the parameter array, followed by the recursively evaluated child results from the remaining entries.

If the number of arguments is outside the range zero through seven, or if the masked type does not match any recognized category, the function returns NaN.

The function attempts to constant-fold an expression node. It first checks whether the node is marked as pure; if not, it returns immediately without changing anything. Otherwise, it determines how many child nodes the node has, then recursively processes each child in order. After processing a child, it checks whether that child is now a constant; if any child is not a constant, the node cannot be folded.

If all children are constants, the function evaluates the node to obtain a numeric result, releases the memory used by the node’s child list, changes the node’s type to the constant type, and stores the computed value in the node’s value field. If any child is not a constant, the node is left unchanged except for any modifications made during the recursive processing of its children.

The function returns nothing. It may free memory associated with the node’s children when folding occurs. The node itself is not freed. The function assumes the argument is a valid pointer to an expression node.

The function compiles a mathematical expression given as a NUL-terminated string into an internal tree representation that can later be evaluated. The first argument is the expression text. The second argument points to an array of variable descriptors; the third argument gives the number of entries in that array. The fourth argument, if not NULL, points to an integer that receives an error indicator.

The function parses the entire expression. If parsing succeeds, it returns a pointer to a newly allocated expression tree, and sets the error indicator, when provided, to zero. The returned tree is owned by the caller and must be released with the provided deallocation helper.

If parsing fails, the function returns NULL. When the failure occurs before any token is consumed, the error indicator is set to negative one. Otherwise, it is set to the zero-based byte offset within the input string where the offending token begins; if that offset would be zero, it is set to one instead. Any partially built tree is released before returning NULL.

The expression may reference variables and functions listed in the supplied descriptor array. The function does not modify the input string or the descriptor array. It may allocate memory for the resulting tree; on allocation failure it returns NULL and sets the error indicator to negative one.

The function evaluates a mathematical expression supplied as a NUL-terminated string and returns the resulting numeric value. The first argument is the expression text. The second argument points to an integer that receives an error indicator if compilation fails; if compilation succeeds, that integer is left unchanged.

The expression is first compiled into an internal representation using the project’s compilation routine, with no external variables supplied. If compilation fails, the function returns the floating-point not-a-number value and stores a nonzero error code in the integer pointed to by the second argument. If compilation succeeds, the compiled expression is evaluated once, the internal representation is released, and the computed value is returned. The second argument is not modified in this case.

The function assumes the first argument is a valid pointer to a NUL-terminated string. It does not check for a null pointer. The second argument may be null; if compilation fails and the second argument is null, no error code is stored. The returned value is a double. On success it is the result of evaluating the expression. On failure it is the not-a-number constant. The function performs no other side effects beyond the temporary allocation and release of the internal representation.

The function ensures that a dynamically allocated array has room for at least one more element, growing it when necessary.

The first argument is a pointer to the array’s data pointer. The second and third arguments point to the current element count and the current allocated capacity, respectively. The fourth argument is the size in bytes of one element.

The function assumes the first three arguments are not NULL, that the current element count does not exceed the current capacity, and that the data pointer is either NULL or a valid allocation compatible with realloc.

If the current element count plus one is less than or equal to the current capacity, the function does nothing and returns zero.

Otherwise, it computes a new capacity: one if the current capacity is zero, otherwise twice the current capacity. It attempts to resize the allocation to the new capacity multiplied by the element size. If the allocation fails, the function returns minus one and leaves the data pointer, element count, and capacity unchanged.

On success, it stores the possibly moved allocation back through the first argument, updates the capacity through the third argument, leaves the element count unchanged, and returns zero. The contents of existing elements are preserved up to the smaller of the old and new sizes. The function does not initialize newly allocated space.

The function ensures that a dynamically allocated array has room for a requested number of elements. The first argument points to the array’s data pointer, the third argument points to its current capacity, and the fourth argument gives the size in bytes of one element. The fifth argument is the number of elements that must fit. The second argument is ignored.

If the requested number of elements is less than or equal to the current capacity, the function does nothing and returns zero.

If the requested number exceeds the current capacity, the function attempts to grow the allocation to hold exactly that many elements. If the allocation fails, it returns minus one and leaves the data pointer and capacity unchanged. If the allocation succeeds, it updates the data pointer to the new location and sets the capacity to the requested number, then returns zero.

The function does not initialize any newly allocated memory, does not change the stored length, and does not free the old allocation separately; the reallocation may move the data, so any previously stored pointers into the array become invalid after a successful call. The first, third, and fourth arguments must be valid pointers, and the element size must be positive.

The function ensures that a dynamically allocated array has enough reserved capacity for a requested number of elements, rounding the request up to the next power of two before delegating the actual reservation work.

The first argument points to the array's data pointer. The second and third arguments point to the current element count and the current allocated capacity, respectively. The fourth argument gives the size in bytes of a single element. The fifth argument is the number of elements the caller wants to be able to store.

If the requested element count is zero, the function returns zero immediately and makes no changes.

Otherwise, it computes the smallest power of two that is at least as large as the requested count. It then asks the underlying reservation helper to grow the array so that its capacity is at least that rounded-up number of elements, passing through the data pointer, the count and capacity pointers, the element size, and the rounded-up count.

The return value is whatever the underlying helper returns: zero on success, or a nonzero error indicator if allocation fails. On failure, the array's existing contents, count, and capacity remain unchanged. On success, the data pointer may be updated to a new allocation, the capacity is increased to at least the rounded-up value, and the element count is left as it was.

The function shrinks the allocation of a dynamic array so that its capacity exactly matches its current length, or releases the allocation entirely when the array is empty.

The first argument points to the array’s data pointer. The second and third arguments point to the array’s current length and capacity, respectively. The fourth argument is the size in bytes of one element.

If the current length is zero, the function frees the existing allocation, stores NULL in the data pointer, sets the capacity to zero, and returns zero.

Otherwise, the function attempts to resize the allocation to exactly the product of the current length and the element size. If the resize fails, the original allocation, data pointer, length, and capacity are left unchanged, and the function returns negative one. If the resize succeeds, the data pointer is updated to the new allocation, the capacity is set equal to the current length, and the function returns zero. The length is never modified.

The function assumes the data pointer, length pointer, and capacity pointer are valid and that the element size is positive. The contents of the first length elements are preserved on success.

The function inserts one new element into a dynamically managed array at a chosen position, shifting later elements to make room. The first argument points to the pointer that owns the array storage. The second argument points to the current number of elements. The third argument points to the current allocated capacity. The fourth argument gives the size in bytes of one element. The fifth argument gives the zero-based index at which the new element slot should be created; it must be within the current element count.

The function first ensures the array has room for one additional element, growing the allocation if necessary and updating the element count and capacity through the pointed-to values. If that growth step fails, the function returns the failure value produced by the growth helper and leaves the array unchanged.

On success, the function moves every element from the insertion index to the end of the array one position toward the end, preserving their order. The memory move is performed as if by the standard byte-copying routine that tolerates overlapping regions. The slot at the insertion index is left uninitialized; the caller is expected to fill it. The element count is not incremented by this function, because the growth helper already accounts for the new element. The function returns zero to indicate success. No other side effects occur.

The function swaps the contents of two elements stored in a contiguous array of fixed-size elements. The first argument points to the array base; the second and third arguments describe the current number of elements and the allocated capacity, but they are ignored. The fourth argument is the size in bytes of one element and must be positive. The fifth and sixth arguments are zero-based indices of the two elements to exchange; they must be valid positions within the array.

If the two indices are equal, the function returns immediately and nothing is modified. Otherwise, the bytes of the two selected elements are exchanged one byte at a time, so the swap is exact even for overlapping or non-trivially copyable element representations. No memory is allocated or freed, no other elements are touched, and the array base pointer, element count, and capacity are unchanged. The function returns no value.
